claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a heterogeneous oxide distribution.
As-received Q235 steel has microstructural variations relevant to corrosion behavior.
Annealing Q235 steel in ambient air at 800 °C for 1 hour will form a uniform Fe-oxide scale.
The Fe-oxide scale formed by annealing will be adherent.
Annealing will reduce grain-boundary segregation near the Q235 steel surface.
High-temperature annealing equilibrates the near-surface microstructure of Q235 steel.
Near-surface equilibration promotes formation of a continuous oxide layer.
The continuous oxide layer limits inward diffusion of corrosive species.
The anneal-formed oxide layer minimizes localized thermal stresses.
The anneal-formed oxide layer reduces stress-induced spallation during cyclic heating and cooling.
The anneal-formed oxide layer preserves corrosion protection at room temperature.
The anneal-formed oxide layer preserves corrosion protection during 700–900 °C salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens will have lower mass gain than as-received specimens during high-temperature Na2SO4 exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens will retain a more coherent oxide scale than as-received specimens during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens will retain a more intact oxide scale than as-received specimens during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens will show improved room-temperature passivation relative to as-received specimens.
The heterogeneous oxide layer on as-received Q235 steel permits greater corrosive-species diffusion.
As-received Q235 steel degrades more rapidly under high-temperature salt exposure than annealed Q235 steel.
The proposed protection is effective only within a narrow window of oxide thickness and phase composition.
Insufficient oxide formation or formation of an excessively thick, brittle scale will reduce corrosion protection.
